title: Task Success Isn't Enough: Connecting Physical AI Safety Research to Engineering Practice
summary: What ASIMOV, SafeVLA-Bench, and RoboHarm reveal about physical AI safety—and how to connect their findings to system requirements, protective measures, and evidence that survives change.
body_markdown:
Imagine a robot carrying a container across a workshop. It reaches the correct bench and puts the container down. The task succeeds. Along the way, it passes too close to a person and destabilizes an object at the edge of another table.


That is an illustrative scenario, but it captures a practical problem: a completion metric can miss the behavior that makes a deployment unacceptable.


Recent physical AI research gives us better ways to examine this gap. Three questions deserve separate attention: **Can the model recognize danger? Does the robot behave safely while acting? What protects people when perception or action fails?** A deployment also needs evidence connecting those answers to a specific system and its operating conditions.


## Recognizing danger is a capability worth measuring


[ASIMOV, introduced in Can AI Perceive Physical Danger and Intervene?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.21651) , studies whether foundation models can recognize physical hazards, reason about constraints, and identify when intervention is needed. Its benchmarking approach draws on injury narratives and operational constraints to construct visual scenarios spanning safe and unsafe conditions.


This is useful because physical safety requires more than recognizing objects. A robot may correctly identify a container, a person, and a workbench while failing to recognize what makes their arrangement dangerous.


For our workshop example, an evaluation could ask whether the model notices the unstable object or recognizes that the planned route creates an exposure. Those are different questions from whether it can identify the destination.


But a correct assessment of a scene does not establish that the complete machine will respond in time. The perception result still has to reach the controller, produce an appropriate response, and change the physical outcome.


## Successful actions can still violate safety constraints


[SafeVLA-Bench](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.00773) adds safety evaluation to existing vision-language-action benchmarks. It uses task-aware temporal constraints to examine behaviors such as excessive contact, disturbance of surrounding objects, and destabilization of held objects. Its metrics distinguish successful completion from successful-but-unsafe behavior.


That distinction changes how a team should read its results. A rising success rate is encouraging, but it cannot answer whether the robot is taking unacceptable shortcuts to finish.


In the workshop, the evaluation should inspect the trajectory and surrounding effects as well as the final placement. Did the container remain stable? Did the robot disturb another object? Were application-specific separation constraints respected?


Those constraints need engineering justification. A simulator's contact threshold is not automatically an acceptable limit for a physical installation. The team needs to explain what each measured quantity represents, how it relates to a hazard, and where the measurement is reliable.


## Refusal in conversation does not establish refusal in control


[RoboHarm, presented in Refuses in Chat, Complies with Arms](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.14043) , examines a different failure mode: harmful instructions. Its experiments compare text and robot-control interfaces, including simulated and physical robot trials, and find that refusal behavior can change substantially across interfaces.


This is distinct from accidental unsafe task completion. An otherwise legitimate request may produce a hazardous trajectory; a harmful request raises the additional question of whether the system should act at all.


Both deserve testing at the interface the deployed system actually uses. A chat evaluation does not cover a controller receiving generated code or motion commands. The paper's results apply to its tested models, interfaces, and scenarios; they motivate deployment-specific evaluation rather than a universal conclusion about every robot.


## Turn a concerning behavior into a system requirement


These projects help expose failures. Engineering practice must then determine how the particular system should prevent or contain them.


For the workshop robot, start with the permitted payloads, routes, human access, sensing conditions, and operating modes. Identify the hazardous situations within that envelope and the consequences of foreseeable failures. Then define protective measures and the evidence required to assess them.


Depending on the application, those measures might include restricted routes, monitored separation, speed limits, guarded areas, or a protective stop. Each has its own assumptions and failure modes. A monitor that detects danger is insufficient if its output is stale, its command is lost, or the machine cannot stop within the available distance.


The useful chain is concrete:


**Hazard → protective measure → requirement → test → result → review decision.**


For example, a response-time requirement needs an allocated budget across sensing, computation, communication, and actuation. Verification needs measurements of that complete path under relevant loads and fault conditions. Neither the budget nor an acceptable stopping distance can be inferred from a model benchmark alone.


## Evaluate the evaluation, then preserve its scope


Evidence also depends on how the evaluation was constructed.[What Are We Actually Benchmarking in Robot Manipulation?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.04233) examines issues including shortcuts, statistical uncertainty, overfitting, and dependence on data sources across manipulation benchmarks.


The practical implication is to ask what a result supports before generalizing it. Which scenarios were held out? Which failures could the scoring method observe? If a learned judge labels unsafe behavior, how was it checked against human review or physical measurements? Where simulation supports a claim, which relevant physical effects have been validated?


A useful evidence record should retain the system configuration, scenario, acceptance criteria, observed behavior, and unresolved limitations. Aggregate scores help with comparison; individual failure traces help engineers decide what to change.


## Safety evidence has to survive system changes


A new policy, camera position, payload, or operating environment can change the relevance of earlier results. Evidence needs a defined scope so a team can identify which assumptions and tests require review after a change.


This is the connection we care about at Saphira: linking analysis, requirements, validation, and change review into a[living body of safety evidence](https://www.saphira.ai/blog/the-safety-case-is-dead-long-live-the-living-safety-case) . The research above offers valuable evaluation methods and failure examples. Applying them to an actual installation still requires system-specific analysis, testing, and engineering judgment.


The next useful conversation is often about one failure trace: what happened, what should have prevented it, what evidence would demonstrate that protection, and which future changes would reopen the question.


That is how a benchmark finding becomes an engineering decision—and how task success becomes one part of a more complete account of robot behavior.
